deviations.claim_in_article: “People asking Muse to call might think AI was calling” and “They did not realize it,” with the surrounding claim that users could not tell whether the caller was AI or a person.
deviations.issue: The article presents users’ actual awareness and experience as facts, and refers broadly to people asking Muse. The Ledger reports inadequate disclosure in a test, but does not establish that users actually believed AI was calling, failed to realize a human was calling, or enjoyed the service unaware.
deviations.explanation: The definite claim that users did not realize a human was calling goes beyond the reported disclosure failure; extending it to people asking Muse also exceeds the employee-test scope. The source article contains the same overstatement.
deviations.qualifier_text: “might think”; “sometimes”; “If no one explained this clearly”

deviations.claim_in_article: “Human staff made inappropriate comments about race during calls. These calls were about trying to lower internet or cable fees.”
deviations.issue: The plural “calls” expands the Ledger’s single reported case into multiple calls. The article retains the fact that this was one employee report, but that qualifier does not establish multiple incidents.
deviations.explanation: The plural calls imply more incidents than the Ledger’s individual reported case; the Japanese source describes a call in the singular, so this expansion arises in translation.
deviations.qualifier_text: “one employee’s report”; “only one report”; “It would be wrong to say all contract workers did this.”
